Abstract INTRODUCTION Identifying at‐risk individuals and selecting sensitive cognitive outcome measures are critical for designing efficient clinical trials targeting early Alzheimer's disease (AD) stages. METHODS We compared amyloid beta (Aβ)‐positron emission tomography (PET), plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p‐tau217), Aβ42/40, and p‐tau217/Aβ42‐related decline across neuropsychological and functional measures in 225 individuals (176 cognitively unimpaired (CU), 49 with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Johnson–Neyman analysis identified the biomarkers, which were used as trial inclusion criteria to estimate sample sizes needed to detect a 30% slowing across cognitive outcomes. RESULTS In the CU, using combined plasma Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217 cut‐offs for eligibility yielded the lowest sample size estimates for a comprehensive multidomain cognitive composite score, whereas sample sizes were higher for all other inclusion criteria based on single biomarkers. In MCI, estimates were substantially lower and less variable across most inclusion criteria and outcome measures. DISCUSSION These findings highlight the need for careful consideration of outcome measures, baseline diagnosis, and inclusion criteria, given their substantial effect on sample size estimation in trials. Highlights Aβ SUVR, plasma p‐tau217, and the p‐tau217/Aβ42 ratio predicted decline across multiple cognitive domains. Using cohort‐specific biomarker cutoffs, sample size estimates were similar for p‐tau217 combined with Aβ42/40 or Aβ SUVR. A multidomain composite best detected AD‐related decline. Predicting cognitive decline with amyloid‐PET, plasma p‐tau217, Aβ42/40, and p‐tau217/Aβ42 in a community‐based cohort – relevance for clinical trial enrollment . Alzheimer's Dement . 2025 ; 21 : e70802 . 10.1002/alz.70802 1 BACKGROUND Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the appearance of neuropathological changes while affected individuals are still asymptomatic. 1 The aggregation and accumulation of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides into extracellular plaques in the brain are among the earliest detectable pathophysiological abnormalities, starting about two decades prior to the onset of clinical symptoms. 2 , 3 However, subtle decline in cognitive performance related to Aβ deposits in the brain can be detected much earlier, 4 providing an early indication of an increased risk of developing clinical AD. Cerebral Aβ plaques can be reliably quantified using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, 5 and recent technical advances have enabled successful quantification of AD biomarkers in blood. 6 The plasma Aβ42/40 ratio and levels of tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p‐tau217) are among the most promising blood‐based biomarkers that distinguish abnormal from normal Aβ status, 7 , 8 , 9 predict Aβ accumulation, 10 and show high performance in predicting cognitive decline. 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 These biomarkers hold significant potential as (pre)screening tools for clinical trials to identify individuals with a high likelihood of Aβ pathology 13 and to enrich the clinical trial population with individuals at increased risk of cognitive decline. 6 , 15 Such a prescreening strategy enhances statistical power and reduces the sample size needed to detect a treatment effect. Another key factor affecting sample size in AD trials is the ability to measure cognitive change sensitively and reliably using optimized outcome measures. Outcome measures that integrate cognition and function, such as the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (CDR‐SoB), have been widely used in past and ongoing AD trials. However, as clinical trials increasingly target Aβ‐positive, cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals, 16 purely cognitive outcome measures may now be more appropriate and informative. Among these, multidomain cognitive composites are currently considered the most sensitive tools for detecting the subtle, gradual decline observed in preclinical and early AD. 17 , 18 The Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC) is one such measure that has been developed to assess the effects of solanezumab – a monoclonal antibody targeting monomeric Aβ – in the Anti‐Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial. 19 , 20 While the PACC is now widely used in research and clinical trials, previous studies indicate that cognitive decline as measured with the PACC is minimal in individuals with intermediate levels of Aβ. 21 , 22 Hence, there remains a need to refine cognitive outcome measures to enable the detection of subtle decline in the very early stages of the disease. The choice of outcome measure, along with the clinical disease stage of the target population, may also influence which biomarker is most relevant for predicting disease progression. 23 Together, these considerations highlight the need for a strategic, disease‐stage‐specific approach to outcome measure and biomarker selection in the design of AD clinical trials. In this study, we investigated how disease stage, cognitive outcome measures, and biomarkers used to predict disease progression interact to influence the sample size required to detect treatment effects in hypothetical clinical trials. We first compared the performance of Aβ‐PET, plasma Aβ42/40, plasma p‐tau217, and plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 in predicting cognitive and functional decline over time in a community‐based sample of older adults. We then investigated how enrollment based on combinations of PET and plasma biomarkers, along with baseline cognitive status and the chosen cognitive outcome measure, influenced sample size estimates required to detect treatment effects.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the predictive performance of amyloid-PET, plasma p-tau217, Aβ42/40, and p-tau217/Aβ42 for longitudinal cognitive and functional decline over 3.5 years in a community-based cohort of 225 older adults, including cognitively unimpaired and mild cognitive impairment individuals. The research assessed how these biomarkers and their specific thresholds impact sample size estimation for Alzheimer's disease clinical trials, concluding that combining plasma p-tau217 with Aβ42/40 or Aβ-PET with p-tau217, alongside multi-domain cognitive assessments, significantly reduces required sample sizes, especially for preclinical Alzheimer's disease.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating biomarker assessment for optimizing Alzheimer's disease clinical trial design and participant selection.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, longitudinal cohort study over 3.5 years, not a therapeutic intervention. Participants were followed annually with cognitive assessments and received baseline biomarker quantification. Aβ-PET imaging utilized approximately 140 MBq [18F]-flutemetamol to calculate global Aβ SUVR. Plasma Aβ42, Aβ40, and p-tau217 were quantified using customized Simoa platforms. The primary focus was on identifying optimal baseline biomarker thresholds (e.g., Aβ-PET SUVR > 1.27 / ~14-34 Centiloids; plasma Aβ42/40 < 0.063; plasma p-tau217 > 1.53 pg/mL; plasma p-tau217/Aβ42 > 0.25) and inclusion criteria to detect a 30% slowing in cognitive decline over 3 years with 80% statistical power in hypothetical clinical trials. No dose-response comparisons for actual treatments were reported.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Imaging (quantification of Aβ plaques, Standardized Uptake Value Ratio - SUVR, Centiloid score)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Predicted decline across multiple cognitive domains. Higher SUVR/Centiloid was associated with faster cognitive decline, particularly in MCI and CU subgroups. A Centiloid > 12 indicated subtle pathological changes. Strongest decline was seen in CERAD delayed recall (β = -0.11, 95% CI: -0.16 to -0.06). Predicted decline in six tasks after FDR correction in the total cohort. Lowest predictive thresholds: MEM-EF-PS (SUVR 1.27, ~14 CL), global composite (SUVR 1.13, ~18 CL), mPACC5 (SUVR 1.43, ~30 CL). In CU, predicted decline in four tasks (CERAD learning and delayed recall, TMT-B, and TMT-B/TMT-A). Sample size estimates using Aβ SUVR as an inclusion criterion were similar to those using combined plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 for detecting a 30% slowing in cognitive outcomes. Optimal predictive ranges of 15 to 18.5 Centiloids were noted for future Aβ accumulation and decline.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Detection and quantification of amyloid-beta aggregation and accumulation into extracellular plaques in the brain, representing early neuropathological changes and a primary pathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of longitudinal cognitive and functional decline over 3.5 years in a community-based sample of older adults (cognitively unimpaired and mild cognitive impairment); used as a criterion for defining biomarker positivity and optimizing clinical trial design for Alzheimer's disease.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reliably quantifies cerebral Aβ plaques, provides an early indication of increased risk of developing clinical AD, predicts decline across multiple cognitive domains, and is crucial for reducing sample size requirements in preclinical AD clinical trials, especially when combined with plasma p-tau217.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Predicted decline across multiple cognitive domains. Stronger AD biomarker abnormality (higher p-tau217) was associated with faster cognitive decline, with strongest decline in CERAD delayed recall (β = -0.10, 95% CI: -0.14 to -0.07). Predicted decline in eight tasks after FDR correction in the total cohort. Lowest predictive threshold for MEM-EF-PS composite was p-tau217 > 1.53 pg/mL. In MCI, strongest decline was in TMT-B (β = -0.17, 95% CI: -0.24 to -0.09). When combined with plasma Aβ42/40, cut-offs yielded the lowest sample size estimates for detecting a 30% slowing in cognitive outcomes in CU individuals. Sample size estimates were similar for p-tau217 combined with Aβ42/40 or Aβ SUVR. Slightly outperformed Aβ SUVR in predicting decline in the total cohort and MCI subsample. Levels below the limit of quantitation (LOQ) were set at LOQ/2 (43% of participants).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Distinguishes abnormal from normal amyloid-beta status, predicts amyloid-beta accumulation, and indicates tau pathology (neurofibrillary tangles) associated with Alzheimer's disease progression.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of longitudinal cognitive and functional decline over 3.5 years in a community-based sample of older adults (cognitively unimpaired and mild cognitive impairment); used as a prescreening tool and eligibility criterion for optimizing clinical trials targeting early Alzheimer's disease stages.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: High performance in predicting cognitive decline, even in preclinical stages; holds significant potential as a (pre)screening tool for clinical trials to identify individuals with a high likelihood of Aβ pathology and enrich trial populations at increased risk of cognitive decline. It is a strong predictor of decline, particularly sensitive to semantic and visuospatial-construction tasks, and highly effective in reducing clinical trial sample sizes, especially when combined with other AD biomarkers.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (ratio of amyloid beta peptides)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Predicted decline across multiple cognitive domains. When combined with plasma p-tau217, cut-offs yielded the lowest sample size estimates for detecting a 30% slowing in cognitive outcomes, particularly effective in preclinical AD. In the total cohort, it was not significantly associated with cognitive decline in most domains, predicting decline in only two tasks after FDR correction. Lowest predictive threshold for MEM-EF-PS composite was Aβ42/40 < 0.063. In MCI, strongest decline was in CERAD delayed recall (β = 0.13, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.21), predicting decline in three tasks after FDR correction. In CU, lower plasma Aβ42/40 predicted faster decline in the Boston Naming Test but was not significant after FDR correction. Single-biomarker use alone resulted in sample size estimates > 5000 per arm in CU individuals.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the processing of amyloid precursor protein and amyloid-beta peptide aggregation in the brain; a lower ratio indicates increased amyloid pathology and distinguishes abnormal from normal amyloid-beta status.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of longitudinal cognitive and functional decline over 3.5 years in a community-based sample of older adults (cognitively unimpaired and mild cognitive impairment); used as a prescreening tool and eligibility criterion for optimizing clinical trials targeting early Alzheimer's disease stages.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: High performance in predicting cognitive decline; holds significant potential as a (pre)screening tool for clinical trials to identify individuals with a high likelihood of Aβ pathology and enrich trial populations at increased risk of cognitive decline. A weaker predictor of cognitive decline compared to p-tau217, but crucial for reducing sample size requirements in preclinical AD clinical trials, especially when combined with p-tau217.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (ratio of phosphorylated tau to amyloid beta peptide)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Predicted decline across multiple cognitive domains. Stronger AD biomarker abnormality (higher ratio) was associated with faster cognitive decline, with strongest decline in CERAD delayed recall (figures) (β = -0.10, 95% CI: -0.15 to -0.05). Predicted decline in seven tasks after FDR correction in the total cohort. Lowest predictive threshold for MEM-EF-PS composite was p-tau217/Aβ42 > 0.25. In MCI, strongest decline was in TMT-B (β = -0.17, 95% CI: -0.24 to -0.10), predicting decline in five tasks after FDR correction. In CU, it did not significantly predict decline in any task, but a threshold for global composite score (p-tau217/Aβ42 > 0.35) was identified.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A composite biomarker reflecting combined amyloid and tau pathologies, integrating information about tau pathology (p-tau217) and amyloid-beta dynamics (Aβ42), potentially offering a more comprehensive indicator of Alzheimer's disease progression than individual markers.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of longitudinal cognitive and functional decline over 3.5 years in a community-based sample of older adults (cognitively unimpaired and mild cognitive impairment); considered for hypothetical clinical trial inclusion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Predicts decline across multiple cognitive domains and worsening CDR-SoB, indicating progression in Alzheimer's disease. Potential improved marker for identifying individuals at increased risk of cognitive decline.
